video_title: Inside Trump's Science Agenda: Anti-Science Claims, Fauci's Damage, DEI & China w/ Michael Kratsios
gist: White House OSTP director Michael Kratsios lays out the 'Science: A New Golden Age' agenda: US research productivity has fallen ~80-fold per dollar since 1950, so the administration is reallocating rather than shrinking the ~$200B federal S&T budget — cutting the ~25% of NSF grants tied to DEI, redirecting climate research after RCP 8.5's withdrawal, and running meta-science experiments (golden-ticket peer review, variable grant lengths, portable fellowships) at NSF and NIH. Hard targets include a scientifically relevant quantum computer by 2028, fusion by 2035, a nuclear reactor in space and boots on the moon by 2028, and the Genesis mission to double US scientific output using AI.

insights.claim: The White House science office argues the binding constraint on US research output is allocation, not appropriation levels — Congress has kept funding science, and OSTP's position is that adding money to the wrong programs is bad policy.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Headline 'science cuts' framing likely overstates the topline risk to research-exposed suppliers; the real dispersion is which programs and institutions get funded, not the aggregate.
insights.quote: spending more money on the wrong types of things is not the right policy action

insights.claim: A Senate committee analysis cited by OSTP found roughly 25% of NSF grants during the Biden administration went to DEI-related work — about $2B a year, or $8B over four years — and that spending is the explicit target of the current reallocation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Sizes the pool of federal grant dollars being redirected (~$2B/yr) and identifies which university programs face defunding versus which get the recycled capital.
insights.quote: roughly one quarter or 25% of grants at NSF during that time period went towards DEI related quote unquote science

insights.claim: The administration disrupted, froze, or terminated $3 billion in unspent funds on already-approved active research grants during 2025.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of realized cash-flow disruption to university research budgets in a single year — relevant to endowment draw and university credit.
insights.quote: in 2025 this administration disrupted froze or terminated $3 billion in unspent funds on active grants

insights.claim: The US government spends about $200 billion a year on science and technology, but OSTP says the sector's lobbying apparatus only ever measures success by whether that number rises, never by breakthroughs per dollar.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: An efficiency-first framing at the top of US science policy means outcome metrics, not budget headlines, will drive the next few years of grant flows.

insights.claim: OSTP's first allocation test is whether the private sector or philanthropy is already incentivized to fund the work — if they are, government should not, pushing federal money back toward basic, pre-competitive discovery research.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: A clean rule for predicting which federal programs survive: anything with a commercial funder gets crowded out of the federal budget.

insights.claim: The first implementation vehicle is the annual R&D priorities memo co-written by Kratsios and OMB director Russ Vought, which directs agencies how to write budgets and puts basic fundamental research on page one.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: The memo is the actual policy instrument to track — it, not the report, determines agency budget submissions.

insights.claim: The top five research agencies — those with over $3 billion in R&D — owe OSTP implementation reports 90 days after publication, and NSF has already announced XLABS to fund focused research organizations plus 4-year industry-partnered PhDs.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: A dated, checkable milestone calendar — agency implementation reports and new NSF program launches are the near-term signals of follow-through.
insights.quote: XLABS announcement coming out of National Science Foundation

insights.claim: Kratsios argues the reform agenda is durable across administrations because its recommendations are nonpartisan and geographically distributive — funding the best scientists anywhere, not just a few northeastern institutions — which builds Congressional support.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Geographic spread of research dollars away from elite northeastern universities is the political mechanism to watch, and a real risk to incumbent institutions.

insights.claim: Asked what happens if the administration loses in 2028, Kratsios's strategy is to run hard for two years and prove the reforms work so that reversing them costs political capital.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Frames a two-year window in which the funding-model changes must show results — the period over which their persistence should be judged.
insights.quote: changing it or turning around is going to be costly from a political capital standpoint because they'll be working

themes.theme: Meta-Science: Rewiring How Grants Are Awarded

insights.claim: NSF and NIH are standing up dedicated 'meta-science' units that will run controlled experiments on funding mechanisms themselves and redirect capital toward whichever mechanisms produce more innovation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: An institutionalized A/B-testing layer on ~$50B of annual grant flow is a structural change that could reshuffle which institutions win money over the next decade.

insights.claim: NSF will test a 'golden ticket' review mechanism — first tried in Denmark — giving each peer reviewer one to three unilateral picks that override committee consensus, explicitly to fund bolder out-of-consensus proposals.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: A deliberate variance-increasing change to US basic research selection; watch for a tail of unconventional grants and, downstream, unconventional startups out of federally funded labs.
insights.quote: each of the evaluators are going to be given one or two or three golden tickets

insights.claim: NSF grants have converged on a de facto 18-month standard set by academic calendars rather than by research need, and OSTP will pilot variable-length grants from 3-6 months up to 5 years.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Shorter fast-track grants create a cheap option-like structure for ideas that currently never get proposed — a new on-ramp for early-stage science.
insights.quote: most NSF grants are roughly 18 months

insights.claim: Consensus peer review structurally selects for low-risk 'in the strike zone' proposals because a scientist's salary depends on winning the grant, which is the opposite of the venture power law where nine of ten failures are the price of one 100x outcome.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind declining research productivity and why VC-style selection is being imported into federal science funding.

insights.claim: NSF's flagship GRFP fellowships — roughly 2,600 a year to top PhD candidates — are fully portable, letting universities compete for the scientist, which OSTP holds up as the model of funding individuals rather than institutions.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Portable funding shifts bargaining power from university administrations to individual researchers, weakening the incumbent-institution moat.
insights.quote: it's totally portable so you can take it anywhere you want

insights.claim: OSTP's stated policy is to fund the best scientist wherever they sit — university, focused research organization, or garage — and it treats academia's read of this as anti-university as a misinterpretation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Non-university research vehicles (FROs, independent institutes) become newly eligible for federal dollars — a funding channel that barely existed before.
insights.quote: We are pro-scientists and we don't care where they are

insights.claim: NIH's budget went from $14B in 1998 to $27B in 2003 to $47B in 2024 — more than tripling — without a proportional rise in breakthrough treatments, and OSTP's director agrees American science has in fact stagnated.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: The head of US science policy conceding stagnation is the precondition for structural reform of the largest biomedical funder in the world.
insights.quote: 1998 14 billion 2003 27 billion 2024 47 billion

insights.claim: Research output per dollar has fallen roughly 80-fold since 1950 and halves about every nine years — an inverse Moore's law the host calls Eroom's law.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the decay rate investors should assume for incremental research spend, and the size of the prize if AI or funding reform bends the curve.
insights.quote: it's fallen roughly 80fold since 1950 50 in terms of outcomes per dollar spent

insights.claim: The median age of an intramural researcher at NIH is 71 years old, a statistic shared with OSTP by NIH director Jay Bhattacharya, and Kratsios hints at coming action to bring young scientists back in.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: A demographic red flag that pre-signals personnel and program overhaul at NIH — watch for announced NIH early-career initiatives.
insights.quote: the median age of an intramural researcher at NIH is 71 years old

insights.claim: OSTP argues stagnation is not mainly low-hanging-fruit exhaustion but institutional non-innovation: agencies kept the same funding method and only added money, because there is no political incentive to audit whether $47B is working.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Frames the reform thesis: the fixable variable is process, and process changes are cheaper and faster than budget increases.

insights.claim: Post-war US science policy still runs on Vannevar Bush's 1945 'Science, the Endless Frontier' model, but the funding mix has fully inverted — from roughly 70% government / 30% private R&D to 70% private / 30% government — which OSTP says makes the Bush model obsolete.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: The single clearest justification for the whole reform agenda; also explains why federal policy increasingly defers to corporate labs on applied work.

themes.theme: Moonshots: Quantum, Fusion, Space, Genesis Mission

insights.claim: A presidential executive order signed last month launched a new national quantum initiative directing the Department of Energy to build a scientifically relevant quantum computer by 2028.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: A hard federal deadline and DOE procurement channel for quantum hardware — a direct demand catalyst for quantum vendors and national-lab suppliers.
insights.quote: create a scientifically relevant quantum computer by 2028

insights.claim: The administration is targeting fusion by 2035 and is actively working to align DOE resources with private-sector fusion investment to hit it.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Public co-funding alongside private fusion capital shortens the runway risk for fusion developers and their supply chains.

insights.claim: Stated space milestones are American boots back on the moon in 2028, a nuclear reactor in space by 2028, and the first elements of a moon base by 2030.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Three dated procurement anchors for space contractors and space-nuclear suppliers over the next five years.
insights.quote: We said we're going to have a nuclear reactor in space by 28

insights.claim: The administration's flagship science program, the Genesis mission, aims to double total US scientific output by applying AI to the hardest problems across materials science, chemistry, math, and physics.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: An all-of-government mandate to embed AI in federally funded research creates a durable government demand channel for AI-for-science tooling and compute.
insights.quote: double the scientific output of the United States by applying AI to our hardest scientific challenges

insights.claim: OSTP explicitly is not trying to compete with private AI spending — the government's role in AI is to push existing basic-research grantees to adopt AI in their work, not to fund frontier model development.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Removes the tail scenario of a federal frontier-AI program competing with labs; federal AI dollars flow to adoption and scientific tooling instead.

insights.claim: The administration's official position is that the climate is changing and human fossil fuel use has contributed CO2, but that the data does not support calling it an emergency — with Energy Secretary Chris Wright as the point person.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Defines the precise policy line: expect no emergency-authority actions, but continued support for energy technology spending.
insights.quote: The thing that is not true and what the data does not support is that it is a climate emergency

insights.claim: Kratsios cites the withdrawal of the RCP 8.5 extreme scenario — which he says could no longer be substantiated with scientific integrity and was pulled from projections — as the central justification for redirecting climate research dollars.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: The specific technical hook the administration will keep using to defend climate grant terminations; expect it to recur in litigation and budget fights.
insights.quote: could not with any scientific integrity substantiate continuing to have this scenario play out

insights.claim: Climate money is being redirected toward abundant-energy technology — nuclear and fusion — on the argument that technology replacing carbon beats policies that raise energy prices, which fall hardest on poorer households.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Federal energy R&D favors nuclear and fusion over climate-impact research; solar and storage are assumed to be solved by market economics without subsidy.

insights.claim: Kratsios argues roughly two billion people still cook with dirty fuels like wood, dung, and charcoal, causing about 3 million deaths a year per UN reporting, so clean fossil fuel access is framed as a humanitarian win rather than a climate loss.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: The moral framing that underpins US support for fossil fuel exports and LNG development to emerging markets.
insights.quote: two billion people around the world use sort of this very dirty fuel

insights.claim: The host argues China's carbon output dwarfs the rest of the world, so a plus-or-minus 50% swing in US emissions does not move the needle, and Kratsios agrees extreme US policy responses would hurt Americans without solving the problem.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: The stated rationale for US climate-policy retrenchment regardless of who holds the White House in the near term.

insights.claim: China's annual science spending went from $33 billion in 2000 to $670 billion in 2021 — a 19x increase — while US spending rose roughly 3x over the same period.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the compounding gap that drives US industrial and export-control policy across chips, quantum, bio, and nuclear.
insights.quote: In the year 2000, China was spending $33 billion a year. 2021 670 billion. So, China increased spending by 19x

insights.claim: The US published roughly twice as many scientific papers as China a decade ago; today China publishes roughly 50% more in nearly every domain except some life sciences.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: Life sciences is flagged as the one remaining US publication lead — the area where US comparative advantage is most defensible.
insights.quote: today, China's publishing roughly 50% more in nearly every domain

insights.claim: Kratsios's strongest evidence that centralized science underperforms is that China has failed to crack EUV lithography since the 2019 export controls despite nothing being more important to its economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Signals the administration believes export controls are working and sees no near-term Chinese EUV breakthrough — supportive of the incumbent lithography monopoly.
insights.quote: EUV lithography since since we put the export controls in 2019. No breakthrough has happened

insights.claim: Kratsios describes China's playbook as copying US IP, producing cheaper alternatives, dumping them into the US market to bankrupt domestic firms, and then squeezing — with critical minerals as the second lever of leverage.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Predicts continued tariff and supply-chain-independence policy in any sector where Chinese price-dumping is plausible; critical minerals stay a priority.
insights.quote: copying our IP, creating cheaper alternatives of that particular technology, dumping them in the United States

insights.claim: The host argues China now gets 2x to 10x more research output per dollar than the US thanks to lower labor costs, more automation, cheaper supply chains, and looser standards — so spending parity understates China's real lead.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: If true, headline spending comparisons systematically flatter the US position, which argues for faster policy urgency than budget numbers suggest.
insights.quote: by some estimates, they get 2x for every dollar they put in

insights.claim: OSTP rejects consolidating US science agencies into a single China-style department, calling America's fragmented, competing agency structure a feature rather than a bug because free-market competition drives breakthroughs.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Kills the recurring 'merge the science agencies' reform thesis — the current multi-agency contracting landscape is stable.

insights.claim: The administration says it must win specifically on AI, quantum, nuclear, and bio, and that the executive branch should hold an explicit thesis about national priorities rather than treating all discovery science as equally worthy.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: A four-sector shortlist for where federal science money and political cover concentrate over the next several years.

insights.claim: US-born share of computer science PhD recipients has inverted over 30 years from roughly 70% American / 30% foreign to the reverse, so about seven in ten STEM PhD candidates in the US are not American.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: The domestic talent shortfall is the structural bottleneck behind both immigration policy tension and long-run US research capacity.
insights.quote: seven out of 10 STEM related PhD candidates in the United States are not American

insights.claim: Kratsios says NSF used to run programs supporting gifted and talented students in American high schools and middle schools, and an active government decision ended them — an outcome he ties to the broader DEI push.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Points to restoration of merit-based gifted programs as a likely near-term NSF policy action.

insights.claim: The host cites San Francisco dropping advanced algebra in high school and the University of California dropping SAT requirements, with Berkeley professors now teaching remedial math and reversing their opposition to standardized testing.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the merit-testing pendulum is swinging back, which would gradually feed the STEM pipeline this administration is targeting.
insights.quote: they stopped one to teach you know advanced algebra to students in high school

insights.claim: Kratsios calls early-career scientists finishing PhDs the most underpaid people in America relative to their national contribution, and makes elevating and rewarding the individual scientist the core tenet of the New Golden Age report.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Expect grant and fellowship design to shift compensation and autonomy toward postdocs and junior PIs, away from institutional overhead.
insights.quote: one of the toughest jobs you can imagine. You're paid almost nothing

insights.claim: On retaining foreign PhDs, Kratsios stops well short of an expanded immigration pathway — the priority order is getting more Americans into STEM first, with legal pathways for those who want to stay as a secondary point.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: Signals no imminent liberalization of high-skill immigration despite the acknowledged talent gap — a persistent constraint for US labs and tech employers.

insights.claim: A Nature poll of 2,000 scientist-readers found 86% supported Kamala Harris and only 6% supported Donald Trump, which Kratsios frames as evidence the scientific community itself has become politicized.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: The scale of the divide explains why institutional resistance to these reforms will be intense regardless of their technical merits.
insights.quote: 86% supported Kla Harris in the election according to the poll and Donald Trump pulled at 6%

insights.claim: Kratsios says Anthony Fauci did more disservice to science than anyone in modern history, citing school masking guidance and pediatric societies endorsing mass protests while barring hospital visits to dying relatives.
insights.speaker: Michael Kratsios, OSTP director
insights.so_what: The administration's science-trust narrative is built on COVID-era credibility loss, which sets the political ceiling for future public health mandates.
insights.quote: he did more disservice to science than than anyone in in modern history

insights.claim: Kratsios says roughly 90% of people hate AI per the host, and while a figure like Demis Hassabis at Google could restore the celebrity-scientist role, the host judges it an uphill battle.
insights.speaker: host (All-In interviewer)
insights.so_what: Public hostility to AI is a live political risk factor for AI-exposed policy and companies, acknowledged inside the White House.
insights.quote: 90% of people hate AI
